name: Dagaare (Dagaari)
catalog_quote: 2.5 Word stress. Finally, we turn to evidence for stress in Dagaare. Our conclusion will be that stress interacts with both lexical and derived tones, yet it can be identified with neither. ... As for Dagaare, we propose that word stress falls on the penultimate syllable.

audit.recode_to: Drop 'fixed-strict'/in the dominant set. reclassify as tone language with analytically inferred, contested foot structure: penultimate (right-edge trochee) per Anttila & Bodomo 1996 vs word-initial trochaic foot with final extrametricality per Anttila & Bodomo 2009/2019, both stating 'little (direct) evidence for stress'. If the schema needs a single pattern, keep penult but not in the strict set, not in the dominant set, grade lowered, and a caution citing A&B 2019 §4.1; the rule string beyond trisyllables (00010, 000010..) is unsupported by any source.
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check passes: both the domain quotation sentences are verbatim in the ROA-169 PDF we hold at printed pp.17-18 (§2.5), and the abstract quote at p.1. (2) The classification rests on a 1996 unpublished OT working paper whose stress claim is a theoretical inference from syllable asymmetries and tone attraction, not a descriptive or instrumental finding. (3) The same two authors subsequently write 'Gur languages are tonal and there is little evidence for stress' (2009 p.56, p.67) and 'There is little evidence for stress in Dagaare' (2019 abstract), and in 2019 posit a word-INITIAL trochaic foot with one final extrametrical syllable — for trisyllables (bá.rʊ́)ʊ́ this puts the head on the antepenult, contradicting the 1996 penult; their 2023 Phonology tone paper no longer uses stress at all. Bodomo's own 2021 LangSci sketch (held) and, per its publisher page, the 2022 JIPA Illustration describe tone only

sources.quote: Abstract: 'There is little evidence for stress in Dagaare, but vowel length alternations in nominal and verbal morphology reveal the presence of a word-initial metrical foot.' §4.1: 'Dagaare words have an initial trochaic foot; feet are binary ...; At most one syllable may be extrametrical: (baa.ʊ)ʊ is possible'. Trisyllables are footed (bá.rʊ́)ʊ́, i.e. foot head on the INITIAL (antepenultimate) syllable, not the penult as in the 1996 ms.
